To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the shape of the displacement interface is highly sensitive to the ratio of the viscosity of the displacing fluid to the viscosity of the displaced fluid and to the permeability and thickness variations in the porous media.

(i) the shape of the displacement front is strongly influenced by cross-sectional variations in channel thickness and permeability, (ii) for small viscosity ratios the flow is focused towards the centre of the domain, (iii) for large viscosity ratios the flow can be focused towards the centre or edges of the domain, and (iv) the shape of a displacement front is strongly dependent on the relative importance of viscous and capillary forces.

cross-channel variations in thickness and permeability in a long channel may lead to the formation of a blunt nose at the leading edge, which is stabilized by capillary pressure, and the remainder of the front becomes stretched out along both edges of the channel.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the flow of two immiscible fluids in a channel whose permeability and thickness vary across the channel.
fluid–fluid displacement, in which one fluid is displaced by a second immi-sible fluid, in a long, thin channel whose width and permeability decrease with distance away from its centreline.
the evolution of the displacement of one immiscible fluid by another fluid through a channel of varying thickness and permeability.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this article presents an analytical model of viscous fingering in a channel of variable thickness and permeability, and compares the model predictions with experimental data.
the present work has shown that the cross-channel variations of the permeability and thickness have a significant impact on the displacement process in a channelled reservoir.
the model is a useful tool to predict the displacement of a viscous fluid in a non-uniform channel, which is of importance to the petroleum industry.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the displacement of one immiscible fluid by another in a channel of varying permeability and width can be described as a topographic viscous fingreting.
the displacement of one immiscible fluid by a second fluid in a long, thin channel with non-uniform permeability and thickness leads to a very complex evolution of the fluid– fluid interface.

we have shown that the cross-channel variation in permeability and width of a long, thin, permeable channel can lead to a very poor sweep of a reservoir by the injected fluid, or a very efficient sweep, depending on the viscosity of the two fluids involved.
The main takeaway from our work is that

if the viscosity of the displaced fluid is much greater than that of the displacing fluid, then the interface will become elongated along the edges of a channel with a non-uniform cross-sectional area, and the displacement will be much more effective.
cross-channel variations in channel thickness and permeability can have a profound effect on the sweep efficiency of a channelled fluid–fluid system.
cross-channel variations in thickness and permeability in a long, thin channel can lead to the partial stabilization of the fluid interface.
